extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, fiction-writers, and students of creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for composing novels: choosing beginning, point of view, scale and length, developing characters over time, selecting illuminating incidents, and matching manner/style to subject. Emphasis on the novelist's choices that make a work feel inevitable, alive and proportioned to its argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent narrative perspective / point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning his tale, the novelist must decide whether it is to be seen through eyes given to noting white moles, or to discovering 'the visionary butterfly alit.' He cannot have it both ways and still hope to persuade his reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a viewpoint (observer focusing on small details vs. imaginative/visionary perception) and keep it coherent; abrupt unmotivated shifts of mind are fatiguing and strain the reader's sense of likelihood (Meredith's parenthetical device worked once but could not be prolonged).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate passage of time naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating the effect of the gradual passage of time so that modifying and maturing of characters seems the natural result of growth in age and experience, not an arbitrary sleight-of-hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest changes in inconspicuous transitional pages that lead from climax to climax; do not fear to go slowly—keep down the narrative tone and be 'as colourless and quiet' as life often is between high moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character continuity through change
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep so firm a hold on the main lines of one's characters that they emerge modified and yet themselves from ripening or disintegrating years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reappearing characters remain recognizably the same despite new lines of suffering and experience (examples: Tolstoy's recurring characters in War and Peace). Use patient, consistent touches to show growth or decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right opening moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The question where to begin is crucial; the art of seizing on the right moment is often more important than presenting many characters at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fixed rule—some subjects demand opening in the heart of action (Henry James), others require gradual ripening (Henry Esmond). The opening must suit the subject and be artistically the real beginning (Balzac's critique of Stendhal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate characters effectively in openings
rubrics_metrics.description: In crowded novels the novelist must 'situate' chief actors so the reader remembers and does not confuse them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different methods work (Tolstoy's sweeping gathering in an opening scene vs. Dostoevsky's gallery of portraits or a gradual ordered introduction like Vanity Fair). The method must suit the subject and justify itself by succeeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length must be determined by the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of a novel needs to be determined by the subject. The novelist should not decide in advance whether to write a long or short novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to be able to say 'It might have been longer,' never 'It need not have been so long.' Length is about the mass and quality of what pages contain and the amount of development the subject requires (examples: Tolstoy, Maupassant, Henry James).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of scale / proportion to argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Know at the start whether one's subject is a small theme (a Salathiel Pavy) or an epic (a Paradise Lost) and proportion characters and scope accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great novelists consistently establish the right relation between subject and length; failing this produces merely long works without intrinsic form (Romain Rolland example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the carrying-power of the theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expand a subject beyond what it can carry; a short flash of horror cannot always be safely stretched into a long novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of overburdening a theme with too much embellishment (examples: Henry James's restraint in The Turn of the Screw; Maeterlinck's overrich prose turning a bee into a 'winged elephant').

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitable ending and thematic closure
rubrics_metrics.description: No conclusion can be right which is not latent in the first page; about the end there should be a clear sense of inevitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather up all threads; any hesitation or failure to resolve shows the author has not let the subject mature. The illuminating incident at the end should meet the light cast forward from the first page (examples: Mme. Arnoux passage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and use of illuminating incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: At every stage the novelist must rely on the 'illuminating incident' to reveal and emphasize the inner meaning of each situation; these are 'the magic casements of fiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illuminating incidents are the author's most direct contribution and best proof of imaginative quality; they give presentness and immediacy and can spare pages of explanation (examples: Julien Sorel taking Mme. Reynal's hand; scenes cited from Flaubert, Eliot, Henry Esmond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor incident over exposition for immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Far more than on dialogue does the effect of immediacy depend on the apt use of the illuminating incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather threads of significance into incidents so explanatory narrative can be minimized. A well-chosen incident can tell in half a page what analysis might take chapters to convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner / style must fit each scene and subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Each tale implies its own manner; the particular shade of style most fitted to convey its full meaning must be found and maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt 'manner' to scene—Stendhal's plain report suits his garden scene, other scenes need different treatment. Variation of manner is legitimate but should be motivated by subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of devices or effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful trick or acrobatic device (e.g., Meredith's parenthetical rendering of thought) can delight once but cannot be prolonged or repeated without straining the reader's patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use striking devices sparingly; genius may allow a one-off flair, but repetition diminishes effect and verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist writing to please popular expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The temptation to keep doing what one knows will be praised is perilous; the fact that many want a writer to write a certain way ought to fill him with distrust of that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating successful formulas simply for popularity; be willing to vary manner and subject even if readers or reviewers desire consistency (critics may pigeonhole authors unfairly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about art — balance theory and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although excessive theorizing can sterilize talent (Henry James warning), thoughtful reflection on the art's range and limitations will usually stimulate and give surer command of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balanced approach: rules and thought can improve workmanship, temper eagerness for popularity, and aid selection, but beware becoming a slave to theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain authorial objectivity over characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist must keep hold on the dual character of his creatures—visionary to him and real to the reader—so he will be the master of his characters, not their slave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should feel alive but remain subject to the consciously imposed world of the creator; do not let genuine emotion in creation (e.g., tears) replace transmutation into artistic substance ('The business of the artist is to make weep, and not to weep').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patience, meditation and concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing the impression of growth and the passing of time requires patience, meditation, concentration and 'all the quiet habits of mind' now seldom practised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate steady habits of mind; genius alone is insufficient without the patient work that makes character development believable over intervals and seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure intrinsic form and unity in long works
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the longest novels must follow a prescribed orbit and be true to an intrinsic form; lack of this form marks a merely long novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the first page communicate the sense of a great theme sweeping on its allotted track. Avoid serial volumes that lack a subtler composition of form proportioned to their setting (Romain Rolland's Jean-Christophe cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin where the subject's art begins (avoid false openings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin before the real beginning of the book; material that is 'real in nature but not in art' is out of place and loses its reality as art (Balzac on Stendhal's Waterloo opening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure every opening scene is integral to the composition; an impressive standalone picture can still be wrong for the specific work if it does not belong to the story's artistic scope.
